message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge a security deposit, but it must be returned within 30 days after you move out, unless you give a written notice of intent to keep it.
• The landlord must provide an itemized list of deductions if any money is withheld. | • Keep a copy of the lease, move‑in inspection sheet, and any receipts for repairs you paid. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to maintain the premises in a habitable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, structural safety).
• The landlord must repair any major defects that affect health or safety. | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep a copy. If the landlord doesn’t fix it, you may be able to withhold rent or repair and deduct. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlords cannot enter your unit without proper notice (usually 24–48 hrs) except in emergencies. | • If a landlord enters without notice, you can ask them to stop and may be entitled to damages. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act and federal Fair Housing laws, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must give notice before the lease ends if they intend to raise rent or change terms. | • Keep a copy of any notice you receive. | | **Rent Increase** | • In a month‑to‑month lease, the landlord must give 30 days’ written notice before raising rent.
• For a fixed‑term lease, the landlord can raise rent only at the end of the lease term. | • Review the lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease violation), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order.
• You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | • Respond promptly to notices, keep records, and consider seeking legal aid if you’re facing eviction. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but you must follow the proper procedure (written notice, reasonable cost, etc.). | • Document the defect, send a written notice, and keep receipts. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlords cannot conduct surveillance or tamper with your personal property. | • If you suspect unauthorized access, document it and report it. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If the landlord pays, they must maintain the service. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Subletting** | • Texas law does not prohibit subletting, but the lease may restrict it. | • Obtain written permission from the landlord before subletting. | | **Legal Assistance** | • Texas has several tenant‑rights groups (e.g., Texas Tenants Union, local legal aid offices). | • Contact them for help with disputes, eviction defense, or lease negotiations. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Note rent amount, due date, security deposit, notice periods, and any special clauses. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, and inspection reports. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – 24–48 hrs for entry, 30 days for rent increase or lease termination. 4. **Report Repairs Promptly** – In writing, and follow up if the landlord doesn’t act. 5. **Keep a Move‑In Inspection Sheet** – Helps avoid disputes over damage when you move out. 6. **Seek Legal Aid Early** – If you receive an eviction notice or face a dispute, contact a tenant‑rights organization or attorney. --- #### Resources - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – Fair Housing complaints: https://www.tchra.texas.gov/ - **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** – Fair Housing: https://www.hud.gov/ - **Texas Tenants Union** – https://texastenantsunion.org/ - **Legal Aid of North Texas** – https://www.lanx.org/ - **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection** – https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/ Feel free to ask if you need more detail on any specific aspect, such as how to handle a security deposit dispute or how to contest an eviction.
